title: Virtues grow (CCC 1804)
hook: virtues are habits built by repeated good acts

segments.voice: Yesterday, forming conscience: a voice to obey, and a voice to teach. Your line was an educated conscience. Did you give some time to the source you picked? Day one thousand one hundred sixteen.

How does someone become honest? Not by one brave decision on a Monday morning. Watch a baker's apprentice in her first week. The dough sticks to the counter, to her fingers, to her sleeves. The loaves come out flat. Every fold takes thought, and most of them go wrong. Then another morning, and another. Somewhere along the way, without anyone marking the moment, something changes. A year on, the same hands fold and turn the dough while she talks about the weather. Nobody gave her that skill in one go. She built it, one sticky morning at a time, until her hands knew before her head did. The Catechism says goodness grows in a person the same way.
screen: `HOW DOES SOMEONE BECOME HONEST?` → `ONE STICKY MORNING AT A TIME.` → `HER HANDS JUST KNOW.`

segments.voice: The word is virtue. The Catechism defines it simply: a habitual and firm disposition to do the good. Not one good deed. A settled way of being, so that good acts come more readily. Then, in the paragraph this day is built on, it describes the human virtues in a string of phrases worth hearing slowly: firm attitudes, stable dispositions, habitual perfections of intellect and will. They govern our actions, order our passions, and guide our conduct by reason and faith. Notice that middle phrase: they order the passions. That picks up two days ago. Feelings aren't sins, but they need a shape, and virtue gives them one. Then the Catechism says what virtue does for the person who has it. It makes possible ease, self-mastery and joy in living a good life. Ease. Like the baker who no longer thinks about her hands. The honest person stops having to argue with themselves every time a lie would be easier. And the virtuous person, it says, is the one who freely practices the good. Then comes the line behind today's title. These virtues, the Catechism says, are acquired by human effort. They are, the Catechism says, the fruit and the seed of morally good acts. Fruit, because good acts repeated build the habit. Seed, because the habit then makes the next good act more likely. A circle that turns toward the good. Saint Paul, quoted by the Catechism just before this, tells the Philippians to think on whatever is true, just, holy and lovely, if there be any virtue. Think on these things, he says. Then, do them.
screen: `A FIRM HABIT OF DOING GOOD.` · `IT GIVES THE PASSIONS A SHAPE.` · `EASE, SELF-MASTERY AND JOY.` · `THE FRUIT AND THE SEED OF GOOD ACTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: repeat one good act. Settle, and breathe. Pick one small good thing you did recently that cost you a little. Holding your tongue. Writing back kindly. Showing up on time. Washing someone else's cup. Picture yourself doing it again today, in the same ordinary way. Then once more tomorrow. Don't aim for something heroic. Aim for something you could do a hundred times. If you pray, you can ask for help to keep at it. If you don't, just decide where and when. The bell holds the time.
Virtue. A firm habit of doing good, built by repeated good acts: the fruit of those acts, and the seed of the next ones. Today's word.
Your line: habits of good. Today, do your one small good act again, and notice whether it's a little easier the second time. Day one thousand one hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: Catholic teaching describes the human virtues as habits acquired by education, deliberate good acts and perseverance, and Catholics work on them through daily practice, the examination of conscience and the sacraments.

original.note: Greek: excellence, virtue — the word in Paul's "if there be any virtue" (Philippians 4:8).

trapdoor: what you thought: virtue means being prim and proper.
what it means: a firm habit of doing good, built by practice, that makes good acts easier and gives feelings a shape.
what a scholar hears: habitual perfections of intellect and will, acquired by human effort, the fruit and seed of morally good acts.

notes: CCC 1803–1804 paraphrased (copyrighted translation): definition (1803), firm attitudes, stable dispositions, habitual perfections of intellect and will; order passions; ease, self-mastery and joy; acquired by human effort; fruit and seed of good acts (1804). Confirm.
Philippians 4:8 paraphrased, with the phrases 'if there be any virtue' and 'think on these things' used without quotation marks; the Douay-Rheims wording could be quoted if a Keeper confirms it.
howItsDone mentions education, deliberate acts and perseverance (CCC 1810), slightly outside the cited range.
Original ἀρετή appears in Philippians 4:8; confirm transliteration.

Audit 2: CCC 1804's sentence reads 'the moral virtues are acquired by human effort' (1810 says human virtues are acquired by education and deliberate acts); the teach now says 'these virtues' rather than putting 'human virtues' inside the Catechism's sentence. Philippians 4:8 phrases match Challoner.
